title: HAGAR THOUGHT HER SON WAS ABOUT TO DIE—Then God Opened Her Eyes to a Well
paragraphs: HAGAR THOUGHT HER SON WAS ABOUT TO DIE—Then God Opened Her Eyes to a Well

She was crying beside a dying son, staring at a wilderness that seemed empty. The water was gone. Hope was disappearing. But Genesis 21:14–19 reveals something hauntingly beautiful: sometimes God's provision is already nearer than your despair allows you to see.
There is a kind of pain that does not scream at first.
It just walks.
One exhausted step after another.
It carries yesterday on its back, uncertainty in its hands, and someone it loves more than itself somewhere beside it.
That was Hagar.
Genesis 21 does not introduce us to a woman sitting peacefully beneath a tree, reflecting on God's goodness while everything in her life makes sense.
It gives us a woman in a wilderness.
Bread.
A skin of water.
A son.
And eventually...
nothing left to drink.
She had already known rejection.
She had already known what it felt like to be caught inside the consequences of other people's decisions.
She had already fled once before and encountered the God who saw her in Genesis 16.
But now she was in the wilderness of Beersheba, and the water was gone.
Read that slowly.
The water was gone.
Not running low.
Gone.
There are moments when faith sounds beautiful because the refrigerator is full, the bills are paid, the children are healthy, and tomorrow still feels predictable.
And then there are wilderness moments.
The doctor calls.
The marriage fractures.
The person you trusted walks away.
The job disappears.
The prayer you have prayed for months seems to return unanswered.
Your child begins fighting a battle you cannot fight for them.
You smile at church while privately wondering how much longer you can keep yourself together.
You know verses.
You know sermons.
You know that God is good.
But your water is gone.
And suddenly theology is no longer something printed on a page.
It is the only thing standing between your soul and despair.
Hagar reached that place.
Genesis says that when the water in the skin was gone, she placed the boy under one of the bushes.
Then she walked away.
Not because she did not love him.
Because she loved him too much to watch what she believed was coming.
She sat about a bowshot away and said, in essence, “Do not let me see the boy die.”
Try to enter that moment without rushing toward verse 19.
Do not run to the well yet.
Sit beside Hagar first.
A mother is looking toward a bush beneath which her son is lying.
Her water is gone.
Her options are gone.
Her strength is gone.
And as far as she can see, the future is gone.
There are prayers we speak beautifully.
And there are prayers made almost entirely of tears.
Hagar wept.
But then Scripture tells us something astonishing.
God heard.
The Hebrew of Genesis 21:17 begins with words worth remembering:
“וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת־קוֹל הַנַּעַר”
Vayishma Elohim et-qol hanna'ar.
“God heard the voice of the boy.”
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not say God finally discovered where they were.
It does not say Hagar's crying alerted an uninformed God to an emergency developing in the wilderness.
God had already spoken concerning Ishmael.

Before Hagar reached this breaking point, God had told Abraham that He would make a nation from his son. The covenant line through which God's redemptive promise would advance was through Isaac; Scripture is explicit about that. Yet God had also declared that Ishmael, because he was Abraham's offspring, would become a nation.
So when Hagar saw death approaching, God had not forgotten His word.
She simply could not see how His word could survive her circumstances.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
You can see the wilderness.
You can see the empty skin.
You can see the bush.
You can see what you lost.
You can see the diagnosis.
You can see the rejection.
You can see the bank balance.
You can see the unanswered message.
You can see the person you desperately want God to rescue.
But you cannot see what God is doing.
And when pain narrows your vision, what you cannot see can begin to feel as though it does not exist.
That is one of despair's cruelest tricks.
Despair takes limited human sight and quietly turns it into a conclusion about an unlimited God.
“I cannot see a way.”
becomes...
“There is no way.”
“I do not understand what God is doing.”
becomes...
“God is doing nothing.”
“I cannot feel Him.”
becomes...
“He has abandoned me.”
But those sentences are not the same.
Hagar could not see a future.
God had already spoken one.
Then heaven addressed her personally.
“What troubles you, Hagar?”
Her name.
In the wilderness.
Her name.
God was not dealing with an anonymous tragedy.
He knew the woman sitting there.
He knew the boy beneath the bush.
He knew the distance between them.
He knew the water was gone.
He knew the fear inside her chest.
And He knew her name.
That matters because suffering has a way of making people feel invisible.
You become “the divorced one.”
“The unemployed one.”
“The addict.”
“The widow.”
“The failure.”
“The person who fell away.”
“The one whose child is struggling.”
“The one who ruined everything.”
“The one nobody checks on anymore.”
But God does not lose your name inside your pain.
The angel of God tells Hagar not to fear because God has heard the boy where he is.
Where he is.
Not where he should have been.
Not where Hagar wished he were.
Not somewhere impressive.
Where he is.
That phrase reaches farther than the wilderness of Beersheba.
God knows where you are.
And even more importantly, the Gospel announces that God did not remain distant from suffering humanity.
The Bible's story ultimately carries us from the wilderness toward Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son of God entered our broken world.
He took on flesh.
He came near to sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He received the rejected.
He called the weary.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
And at the cross, Jesus did something infinitely greater than merely improving difficult circumstances.
He dealt with our deepest catastrophe.
Sin.
Our greatest need is not merely for God to make our wilderness comfortable.
Our greatest need is reconciliation with the God against whom we have sinned.
We do not simply need better circumstances.
We need forgiveness.
We need mercy.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners and rose again.
The Gospel is not that good people eventually find enough strength to walk out of the desert.
The Gospel is that the Son of God came to save people who could never save themselves.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin through Christ and offering forgiveness to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
And perhaps that is the well someone reading this has never seen.
You have been asking God to fix your money, your relationship, your loneliness, your career, your anxiety about tomorrow...
while Jesus is calling you to something deeper than temporary relief.
Himself.
Because you could receive everything you have ever wanted and still die spiritually thirsty.
You could gain applause and remain empty.
You could rebuild your reputation and remain unreconciled to God.
You could fill your house and still have an empty soul.
The greatest gift God can give you is not a life in which you never enter a wilderness.
It is Himself.
Then comes one of the most unforgettable sentences in Hagar's story.
Genesis 21:19 says:
“וַיִּפְקַח אֱלֹהִים אֶת־עֵינֶיהָ”
Vayifqach Elohim et-eineha.
“Then God opened her eyes...”
And she saw a well of water.
Think about that.
The text does not describe Hagar digging the well.
It says God opened her eyes and she saw it.
One moment she believed she was sitting near the end of her son's life.
Then her eyes were opened.
Water.
A well.
Provision.
Hope.
She went to it, filled the skin with water, and gave the boy a drink.
The wilderness had not instantly disappeared.
But now she saw something in the wilderness she could not see before.
That is the line I cannot shake:
God opened her eyes.
Because sometimes the miracle you desperately need is not God explaining every unanswered question.
Sometimes it is God opening your eyes to what is true while you are still standing in the wilderness.
Maybe the well is a brother or sister in Christ you have been too ashamed to call.
Maybe it is the church community you keep avoiding because hiding feels safer than being known.
Maybe it is repentance you have postponed because surrender would mean admitting you were wrong.
Maybe it is forgiveness you know you need to seek.
Maybe it is Scripture you stopped opening because disappointment made you distant.
Maybe it is help you were too proud to ask for.
Maybe it is simply the realization that God's silence is not proof of God's absence.
But we must be careful here.
Genesis 21 is not a formula promising that every illness will be cured, every marriage restored, every financial crisis immediately reversed, or every wilderness removed in the way we want.
Faith does not mean forcing Hagar's exact outcome onto every tragedy.
Some faithful Christians have prayed through tears and still buried someone they loved.
Some have trusted God and still lost jobs.
Some have obeyed Christ and still suffered deeply.
Jesus Himself told His followers that they would have trouble in this world.
Christian hope is stronger than the promise of comfortable circumstances.
Our hope is Christ.
The crucified Christ.
The risen Christ.
The reigning Christ.
The Christ who forgives sinners.
The Christ who remains faithful.
The Christ who will finally make all things right.
The Christ who conquered death itself.
Hagar's well therefore points us toward a larger biblical reality: human vision is limited, but God's faithfulness is not.
Your empty water skin does not empty God of His power.
Your confusion does not confuse Him.
Your tears do not embarrass Him.
Your wilderness does not place you outside His sight.
And your past does not possess more saving power than the blood of Jesus Christ.
That last truth may be the one somebody desperately needs.
Because perhaps your wilderness is partly of your own making.
Maybe you did make the decision.
Maybe you did betray someone.
Maybe you did relapse.
Maybe you did lie.
Maybe you did compromise.
Maybe you did waste years.
Maybe nobody forced you.
Maybe when you look backward, you cannot blame anyone else.
The Gospel does not require us to rewrite our history and pretend our sins were virtues.
It does something far more glorious.
Jesus can redeem sinners who finally stop hiding.
Repentance says, “Lord, I have sinned.”
Grace says, “Christ is sufficient for repentant sinners.”
Faith stops defending itself and runs toward Jesus.
That is why shame does not get the final sentence.
That is why failure does not get the final sentence.
That is why your worst chapter does not automatically become your final chapter.
From scandal to grace...
because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by pretending rebellion was obedience.
Not by erasing truth.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking guilty people, washing them by grace, reconciling them to God, and transforming their lives.
He turns rebels into sons and daughters.
He turns hidden sin into confessed sin.
He turns condemnation into justification for those who are in Him.
He turns graves into places from which resurrection hope speaks.
And maybe while reading this, you realized something uncomfortable.
You have spent months asking God to change what is around you while resisting what He wants to change within you.
You want the well.
But do you want God?
You want relief.
But do you want repentance?
You want restoration.
But do you want surrender?
You want Jesus to rescue the life you designed.
But are you willing to let Jesus become Lord of it?
Because someday the things consuming you right now will no longer matter.
The applause will stop.
The money will belong to somebody else.
The house will have another owner.
Your social-media profile will become silent.
Your achievements will become memories.
And you will stand before God.
The question will not be whether you looked Christian enough online.
The question is whether you belong to Christ.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you have been running, turn around.
If you have been playing with sin, repent.
If you have been trying to earn salvation, stop trying to purchase what Christ alone can provide by grace.
Call upon Jesus.
Trust Him.
Bring Him the truth about you.
Not the edited version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version everybody follows online.
You.
The frightened you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The exhausted you.
The you sitting a bowshot away from something you cannot bear to watch die.
Come to Christ.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn conviction into another moment you merely consume and forget.
Someone reading beneath you may be sitting in the place where you once sat.
Your story may remind them that despair does not know everything.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person whose smile has looked different lately.
The mother fighting quietly for her child.
The father carrying pressure nobody notices.
The believer who has become distant.
The friend who says, “I'm fine,” a little too quickly.
The person who has never trusted Christ.
Saving it helps too.
There are words you understand differently when the water runs out.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith and you want to help this work continue and expand, there is another way to stand with the mission.
The New Testament says giving is not to be done reluctantly or under compulsion, but from a willing heart.
If this ministry has helped you, consider helping us keep helping others.
Not because God needs your money.
Not because salvation has a price tag.
But because ministry requires people willing to pray, share, serve, give, create, send, and stand together.
If you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior reach farther?” this is one tangible answer.
It is people.
Another exhausted believer.
Another searching soul.
Another person reading alone at 2:00 in the morning.
Another marriage desperate for biblical truth.
Another prodigal who needs to remember the Father's mercy.
Another Christian who needs discipleship instead of another empty motivational slogan.
Another person in a wilderness who cannot see the well yet.
Send it privately to someone.
Pray that Jesus Christ—not a page, not a personality, not an algorithm—would be magnified through every word.
Because the goal is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The goal is to make Christ known.
Hagar believed she was about to watch her son die.
She could see the empty container.
She could see the wilderness.
She could see the bush.
She could see everything that frightened her.
Then God opened her eyes.
And there was the well.
Perhaps tonight you still do not know how your story turns out.
Perhaps the prayer has not been answered the way you hoped.
Perhaps nothing around you has changed since you began reading.
But do not confuse what you cannot see with what God cannot do.
Do not build your theology entirely from the contents of an empty water skin.
Do not let one terrible chapter convince you that God has stopped being God.
Look again toward Christ.
Open the Scriptures again.
Pray again.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask for help.
Tell somebody the truth.
And when fear whispers, “This is where everything ends,” remember a crying woman in the wilderness whose eyes could not yet see what God already knew was there.
The water skin was empty.
God was not.
And maybe that is the sentence you need to carry into your wilderness:
What looks like the end from where you are standing may still be the place where God teaches you to open your eyes and look toward Him.
